subject: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes

messages.author: 7bdd454e07081825
messages.subject: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes
parts:
Dear group,

I was hoping someone could advice me on the possibilities to use genomic SEM beyond human disease and crop breeding. Specifically, I am wondering what minimum sample sizes are recommended to run genomic SEM with adequate power. 

The studies I have found to date that use genomic SEM all have the privilege of working with human or plant data that contain over thousands of samples. However, these sample sizes are less common within ecology, although this approach would be of great use to identify genetically correlating traits in our field too. Therefore, I was wondering if there are any rules-of-thumb for conducting genomic SEM with regards to sample size and maximum number of traits one could test with it. Is it of any use to use this approach with sample sizes lower than 1,000?

Many thanks,
Rebecca

messages.author: d88de118c479e0b6
messages.subject: Re: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes
parts:
Hi Rebecca,

Because Genomic SEM relies heavily on the implementation of LDSC, (at least for human data) the minimum sample size is likely around 5000 effective sample sizes. Neale lab also found that for UK Biobank data ~4500 effective sample size was required for "80% power to detect h2 ≥ 0.2 at nominal significance (p<.05)". You might be able to get better precision with lower sample size using HDL as noted here, but again this is all on European human data and it would require you to generate a separate reference panel. 

Is there a way to calculate the heritability Z-score for your data? h2 Z > 4 is recommended for Genomic SEM I think.

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: Using genomic SEM in ecology: advice on minimum required sample sizes
parts:
old thread, sorry for the slow response. I think it depends highly on the genetic architecture of your trits in a given species. 

Some prerequisites: 

1. would you technically  be able to do LD score regression in your species? 
- do you have sequence data for sufficient samples to make LD scores
- are the traits polygenic enough where ld score will work

2. If you can technically because you have the right kind of data, does LDSC heritability agree generally with GREML or pedigree based estimates of h2?

If the SEm models are of interest and ou have either pedigree data or have shown REML to work then there are some non GHenomicSEM options I could recommend.
